excerpt: Resigning does not automatically end workers' comp benefits in Georgia or South Carolina — but it puts wage replacement at risk. What actually changes.
keyTakeaways: Resigning while on workers' comp does not automatically end your benefits, but it creates risks. Medical benefits continue regardless of employment status in both Georgia and South Carolina. Wage replacement benefits are vulnerable — insurers will invoke the voluntary limitation of income defense (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-240) or unjustified refusal (S.C. Code § 42-9-60). Constructive discharge preserves benefits. Before resigning, consult an attorney, get your doctor's restrictions documented, and consider waiting until after your impairment rating.

faqs.question: Will I lose my workers' comp benefits if I resign?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Workers' compensation benefits are tied to your work-related injury, not your employment status. Medical benefits continue regardless of resignation. Wage replacement benefits (TTD and TPD) may continue if your wage loss is due to the injury rather than your choice to leave, but the insurer will likely argue your income loss is voluntary.

faqs.question: Do medical benefits continue after I resign from my job?
faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-200) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-15-60), the employer's workers' comp insurer must continue covering all reasonable and necessary medical treatment for the work injury regardless of your employment status. This includes doctor visits, surgery, physical therapy, and prescriptions.

faqs.question: What is the 'voluntary limitation of income' defense?
faqs.answer: In Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-240), the insurer can argue that you are voluntarily limiting your income by resigning from a job you were capable of performing. If the workers' comp board agrees, your wage replacement benefits can be suspended. The burden is on the insurer to prove suitable work was available within your restrictions.

faqs.question: What if I resigned because my employer was retaliating against me for filing a claim?
faqs.answer: This may qualify as constructive discharge, which is treated as involuntary termination — preserving your wage benefits. Both Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-17) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 41-1-80) prohibit employer retaliation for filing workers' comp claims. Document all incidents of retaliation before resigning.

faqs.question: Can I take a new job while receiving workers' comp benefits?
faqs.answer: Yes, but it affects your payments. If the new job pays equal to or more than your pre-injury wage, TTD benefits end. If it pays less, you may receive TPD benefits for the difference. Medical benefits continue regardless. You must report new employment to the insurer — failing to disclose income can result in fraud allegations.

faqs.question: What happens if I refuse a light-duty job offer and resign instead?
faqs.answer: This is one of the highest-risk scenarios. The insurer can argue you refused suitable employment, triggering benefit suspension under Georgia's O.C.G.A. § 34-9-240 or South Carolina's S.C. Code § 42-9-60. Before refusing, have an attorney evaluate whether the job is genuinely within your restrictions and offered in good faith.
